extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, comparative politics, and civic education
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria for what sustains or undermines democratic (particularly Anglo‑American) institutions — focusing on religion, instruction, laws, manners, and practical experience. The excerpt distinguishes causal roles and prescriptive features for maintaining democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two great dangers to religion: schism and indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: The two great dangers which threaten the existence of religions are schism and indifference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schism: in fervent ages people abandon one religion to adopt another, producing continued religious passion or enmity. Indifference: negative doctrines that deny the truth of one religion without affirming another secretly undermine faith; people desert religious opinions from lukewarmness rather than active dislike, losing the sentiments that once fostered belief and ending in scepticism and despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy renouncing state support preserves religion's lasting influence
rubrics_metrics.description: American clergy 'saw that they must renounce their religious influence, if they were to strive for political power; and they chose to give up the support of the state, rather than to share in its vicissitudes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By refusing to be political allies of state authority, clergy avoid being identified with decaying powers and thus maintain religion's independent and enduring moral influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative undermining of religion leads to concealment and social tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: When unbelievers regard religion as useful but not true, they conceal their incredulity; believers openly avow faith and view nonbelievers with pity rather than opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This social dynamic produces public opinion favorable to religion even when private belief declines; the mass instinct for a future life sustains outward religious practice despite internal wounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction, habits, and practical experience promote success of democratic institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The instruction, the habits, and the practical experience of the Americans promote the success of their democratic institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary instruction is widespread (e.g., New England: basic knowledge, religion, history, constitution). Practical experience (governing by participation) is more serviceable than book‑learning: 'The American learns to know the laws by participating in the act of legislation.' Education should awaken understanding and be combined with moral education to support a democratic republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical experience matters more than book learning for citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: True information is mainly derived from experience, and book-learning alone does not instantly make citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Americans are often 'more superficially instructed' but obtain civic competence through gradual self-government; instruction prepares for ideas but does not furnish the practical notions — governing produces practical civic knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners are the principal cause for maintaining democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners (moral and intellectual characteristics of a people collectively) are more influential in maintaining democratic institutions than laws or physical circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manners comprise habits, opinions, convictions, religion merged with liberty, and practical experience; these permeate daily life and law, and can overcome unfavorable geography or imperfect laws. The author ranks causes: physical circumstances < laws < manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be adapted to the people and country but are subordinate to manners
rubrics_metrics.description: American legislation, taken collectively, is extremely well adapted to the genius of the people and the nature of the country; but laws are subordinate to manners and are not always universally applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well‑designed laws (e.g., federal laws) cannot ensure democratic success if manners are adverse (example: Mexico adopted similar laws but could not maintain democracy). Laws should fit national character and conditions, yet remain insufficient alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical circumstances alone are inadequate to secure democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical causes (territory, resources, isolation) are inadequate to produce results analogous to the United States without appropriate laws and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison with South America: similar or superior physical endowments did not prevent misery where laws and manners differed. Thus geography cannot substitute for civic customs and legal frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic institutions must be gradually mixed with habits and opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic institutions introduced prudently and gradually so they mix with habits and are infused into opinions of the people can subsist elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transplanting American institutions wholesale into different social/political contexts (e.g., Europe) would require modification; a democracy can be organized differently (more centralized executive, etc.) but must be slowly integrated with popular habits to endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional civic formation affects stability: eastern vs western states
rubrics_metrics.description: Eastern states show vigor, regularity, wisdom and durability in republican government; western states often display irregularity and feverish excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences attributed to length of practice with democratic governance, level of instruction, religious morality, density of social ties; western populations may combine 'savage' frontier habits with inherited civilisation, producing more intense passions and less stable convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid circulation of public opinion and communication infrastructure promotes enlightened citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in remote frontiers public opinion circulates rapidly via the post and newspapers; this facilitates the diffusion of elementary instruction and civic knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: frontier 'postoffices' and bundles of letters/newspapers kept isolated settlers informed; such communication substitutes for concentrated urban education and aids democratic functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social equality of settlers aids democracy but is not alone sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Anglo-Americans settled in a state of social equality (absence of entrenched aristocracy) which assisted the establishment of democracy, but similar equality existed in other transatlantic colonies which did not maintain democratic institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore social equality is a facilitating condition but must be accompanied by appropriate laws and, crucially, manners to sustain a democratic republic.
